title: Plugging In, Charging Ahead: Comparing EU and Canadian Approaches to Chinese Investment in the Electric Vehicle Sector
gist: The EU is pivoting to a rules-based conditionality model for Chinese EV investment — centered on the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act requiring prior authorization for >€100m investments from countries holding >40% of global sector capacity — while Canada has traded 100% EV tariffs for a 49,000-unit quota at 6.1% (in exchange for Beijing cutting canola duties from ~84% to ~15%) and is courting investment via four soft 'guiding principles'. Chinese firms are frontloading into welcoming EU markets (2025 FDI €16.8bn, automotive €7.6bn, +46%, 93% EV-supply-chain) while approving nothing in Canada, where USMCA uncertainty and new US 50% Section 338 tariffs make Canadian production a poor bet.

insights.claim: Canada agreed in January 2026 to admit 49,000 Chinese EVs annually at a most-favored-nation tariff rate of 6.1% — roughly 3% of Canada's vehicle market — replacing the 100% tariffs Ottawa imposed in August 2024.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: First G7 rollback of prohibitive Chinese EV tariffs; sets a precedent and a size benchmark (3% of market) other countries may copy.
insights.locator: Canadian Prime Minister Carney's visit to Beijing in January 2026

insights.claim: The Canadian EV quota was granted in exchange for Beijing slashing retaliatory tariffs on Canadian canola seed from roughly 84% to about 15% and easing curbs on other agricultural exports, an explicit agriculture-for-autos trade.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Reveals the exchange rate Beijing sets between farm-export relief and auto-market access — a template for other agricultural exporters facing Chinese duties.
insights.locator: During the trip, Canada agreed to admit 49,000 Chinese EVs

insights.claim: Canada's EV quota requires at least half of imported vehicles to be 'affordable' — under CAD 35,000 (US$24,900) — by 2030, and expands 6.5% per year to a maximum of 70,000 vehicles annually by that date.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Puts a hard price ceiling into a Western market: cheap Chinese EVs get a legally protected entry channel that will pressure incumbent OEM pricing in Canada.
insights.locator: Importantly, the EV quota included provisions

insights.claim: The Canadian quota took effect March 1, 2026 for an initial six-month period while Ottawa sought public input on a longer-term allocation system to begin September 1, meaning the regime's durability is an open decision point this autumn.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete September 1 catalyst date for Canada-China EV trade policy.
insights.locator: The quota took effect on March 1, 2026

insights.claim: Chinese-produced EVs began arriving in Canada in May 2026 but most appear to be Western brands manufactured in China, such as Tesla, so Canadian consumer reception of Chinese brands remains untested.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Early import data overstates Chinese-brand penetration; the real demand test comes later, and Tesla is the near-term beneficiary of the quota.
insights.locator: On the trade front, Chinese-produced EVs started arriving in Canada in May

insights.claim: Tesla had equipped its Shanghai Gigafactory in 2023 to produce a Canada-specific Model Y but halted those shipments and shifted Canadian supply to its US and Berlin factories after Ottawa's 2024 100% tariff, showing how quickly tariff regimes rewire single-model sourcing.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that plant-level sourcing decisions are tariff-elastic within one to two years — relevant for modelling any tariff reversal.
insights.locator: Tesla had already prepared in 2023

themes.theme: Joly's four principles and their conspicuous gaps

insights.claim: Canada's Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has set four guiding conditions for approving Chinese EV investment: a majority Canadian-owned joint venture, labor standards aligned with Canada's existing auto industry, sourcing from localized Canadian supply chains, and secure vehicle software with user-data protection.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The de facto approval checklist for any Chinese auto investment in Canada — deals structured outside it are unlikely to clear.
insights.locator: For the time being, Minister Joly has put forward four guiding principles

insights.claim: Technology transfer and intellectual-property licensing are conspicuously absent from Joly's four Canadian conditions even though they are central to the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, meaning Canada is not currently bargaining for Chinese technology.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Canada risks getting assembly jobs without capability transfer — the key differentiator when comparing long-run industrial payoff between the EU and Canadian models.
insights.locator: Certain categories of conditions are also conspicuously missing

insights.claim: Despite Joly's stated preference for majority-Canadian joint ventures, she has also said she wants Canadian companies doing contract manufacturing for Chinese EV makers — as Magna International does for Xpeng in Austria — a model analysts note is not a joint venture and centers on assembly rather than substantive technology or IP transfer.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Internal inconsistency in Canadian policy signals to investors; Magna-style contract assembly is the most likely actual outcome, which is a modest revenue win, not an industrial-policy win.
insights.locator: Joly has also suggested she wants to see Canadian companies engaged in contract manufacturing

insights.claim: Joly ruled out Stellantis' proposal to assemble Leapmotor EVs from 'knock-down kits' at the idled Brampton, Ontario plant, stating plans must be supported by the provincial government and the workers' union — establishing union and provincial consent as de facto veto points.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Any Canadian assembly proposal must be pre-cleared with unions and provinces; kit assembly specifically is off the table.
insights.locator: As one example, Stellantis suggested partnering with Chinese automaker Leapmotor

insights.claim: BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said a joint venture would not work for BYD because of the company's vertical integration and that BYD would insist on owning and operating any Canadian facility outright, putting the largest Chinese EV maker in direct conflict with Ottawa's majority-Canadian-JV requirement.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Structural impasse: the biggest potential investor's business model is incompatible with the host country's headline condition, so expect no BYD Canada plant absent a policy change.
insights.locator: Separately, BYD's Executive Vice President Stella Li said

insights.claim: Despite Joly's June 2026 Shanghai meetings with BYD, Chery, Geely and Shanghai Launch Automotive Technology, no major Chinese automotive investment in Canada has formally moved forward, and Canada retains final approval authority under the Investment Canada Act's 'net benefit to Canada' test.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Zero deals approved after six months of courtship is the cleanest scoreboard on whether soft signalling attracts capital — so far it does not.
insights.locator: Following her June meetings with representatives from BYD

themes.theme: The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act conditionality

insights.claim: The EU's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, introduced March 2026, would require prior authorization for investments above €100 million (US$114 million) in emerging strategic sectors such as EVs when the investor comes from a country controlling more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in that sector — a threshold widely understood as aimed at China.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified screening trigger — the €100m/40% test is the number to model when assessing which Chinese cleantech projects need EU pre-approval.
insights.locator: At the center of the EU's investment strategy is the IAA

insights.claim: Qualifying investments under the IAA would have to accept limits on foreign ownership, joint ventures with European partners, technology transfer, EU-based R&D, local sourcing and domestic employment commitments — a full industrial-policy conditionality package rather than a security screen.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Defines the cost of EU market access for Chinese cleantech capital; margin-dilutive conditions that could push investment toward looser jurisdictions.
insights.locator: Qualifying investments would be required to fulfill specific conditions

insights.claim: The IAA still requires approval by the European Parliament and Council with adoption not expected before 2027, and diverging member-state interests may water down or delay it.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A multi-year regulatory window in which pre-IAA investments can be locked in — the timing arbitrage driving current Chinese FDI behaviour.
insights.locator: The proposal still requires approval by the European Parliament

insights.claim: The EU's internal fight is between prioritizing products 'Made in Europe' versus those 'Made by Europe', with France leading governments favouring the latter while Sweden and the Czech Republic warn buy-local requirements could deter investment, raise government tender prices and hurt EU competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The Made in/Made by split determines whether Chinese-owned EU plants count as European supply — the single most consequential definitional fight for EV supply chains.
insights.locator: A key debate centers on whether the policy should prioritize products

insights.claim: The EU imposed countervailing tariffs on Chinese EVs ranging from 7.8% to 35.3% in 2024, and in January 2026 opened a pathway for exporters to seek relief via minimum-price commitments — but only Volkswagen's Cupra has been approved so far, leaving the tariffs largely in place.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Minimum-price undertakings are the individual escape hatch from EU EV duties; each approval is a company-specific margin event worth tracking.
insights.locator: Using tools intended to offset unfair subsidies

insights.claim: Beyond the IAA the EU is considering supplier-concentration ceilings of roughly 30% to 40% for any single supplier, with remaining components sourced from at least three suppliers not all from the same country — a structure aimed squarely at diversifying away from China.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Would force multi-sourcing over cost efficiency and complicate vertical integration even for EU-based firms; a structural margin headwind for European manufacturers.
insights.locator: Another policy that has been floated would set ceilings

insights.claim: Under proposed Cybersecurity Act revisions the EU plans to phase out components from 'high-risk' suppliers in critical sectors likely to include EVs, and China's Chamber of Commerce to the EU claims this could cost the bloc more than $400 billion over five years, with Germany bearing nearly half the burden.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A quantified (if self-interested) estimate of rip-and-replace costs concentrated in Germany — relevant to German industrial capex and asset write-downs.
insights.locator: In addition, under proposed revisions to its Cybersecurity Act

insights.claim: China's Ministry of Commerce has publicly labelled the IAA discriminatory and a violation of fair competition, raised it at the WTO, and in early May threatened countermeasures against the EU over the Cybersecurity Act unless substantial changes are made.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Escalation risk is two-sided: EU conditionality invites Chinese retaliation against European exporters, a channel to watch for German autos and machinery.
insights.locator: Chinese officials contest policies as overly restrictive

insights.claim: Most decisions on attracting, approving or conditioning foreign investment still sit with EU member states, because the 2019 FDI Screening Regulation only coordinates national reviews and recent updates merely mandate all member states adopt screening mechanisms by 2028.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Until 2028 the binding constraint is national politics, not Brussels — so member-state elections are the real approval variable for Chinese projects.
insights.locator: Decisions about whether to attract, approve, or condition

themes.theme: Chinese FDI frontloading into welcoming markets

insights.claim: Chinese FDI into Europe reached its highest level since 2018 in 2025 at €16.8 billion (US$19.1 billion), with nearly half flowing into the automotive sector and EV supply chains.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Hard number showing Chinese capital is entering Europe at a seven-year high precisely as restrictions are being drafted — the opposite of the deterrence narrative.
insights.locator: In 2025, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) into Europe

insights.claim: Chinese automotive investment in Europe totalled €7.6 billion (US$8.6 billion) in 2025, a 46% increase from 2024, with 93% of it focused on the EV supply chain.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The 93% concentration figure shows Chinese European capex is essentially a pure EV-supply-chain bet — a leading indicator for European battery and component capacity additions.
insights.locator: The automotive sector attracted the most investment

insights.claim: Chinese investment concentrates in politically welcoming EU markets: Hungary attracted €3.8 billion (US$4.3 billion) in 2025, Spain's inbound Chinese FDI rose 147% and Germany's rose 88%.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Political welcome, not subsidies or market size, is the strongest predictor of where Chinese EV capital lands — a screen for regional industrial-property and supplier plays.
insights.locator: Most investments are concentrated in markets that offer a political welcome

insights.claim: Firms investing in the EU now could gain a competitive advantage over those later subject to the IAA's strict conditions, so the prospect of new rules is itself accelerating Chinese investment rather than deterring it.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive policy effect: announcing future restrictions pulls capex forward and grandfathers incumbents — expect an investment rush ahead of 2027.
insights.locator: If the IAA is adopted, those firms that invest now

insights.claim: Chinese EV manufacturing in Europe is only now reaching production: BYD's €3.8 billion (US$4.3 billion) Szeged, Hungary plant is close to operation with full-scale production slated for end-2026, and Stellantis-Leapmotor will produce the Leapmotor B10 at Zaragoza, Spain from the second half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: H2 2026 to end-2026 is when locally made Chinese EVs actually hit European showrooms — the demand test and the pricing shock arrive together.
insights.locator: Even with these trends, the status of Chinese-invested facilities

insights.claim: CATL committed €7.34 billion (US$8.3 billion) in 2022 to a 100GWh battery plant in eastern Hungary aimed at supplying the European market, and existing Chinese investments there are likely to stay even though Budapest is expected to be more circumspect toward Beijing under new prime minister Péter Magyar.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sunk Chinese battery capacity in Hungary is politically irreversible — a durable European cell-supply asset regardless of the change of government.
insights.locator: Hungary was an early favorite destination

insights.claim: Spain has become the new magnet after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's April 2026 Beijing trip, with a Stellantis-CATL LFP battery joint venture at Zaragoza starting production end-2026, Chery's €400 million (US$456 million) joint venture with EV Motors in Barcelona, a Hithium battery-storage gigafactory, SAIC Motor's first EV plant in Galicia, and MingYang reportedly eyeing Spain after the UK rejected its investment.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Spain is the concentrated expression of the 'political welcome' trade across batteries, EVs, storage and wind — watch Spanish industrial and grid supply chains.
insights.locator: More recently, Chinese companies have rushed toward Spain

insights.claim: Ford, Nissan and Volkswagen have all discussed letting Chinese firms such as Geely and BYD use idle capacity at their European plants, as the Western OEMs wrestle with sluggish demand and high production costs.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Idle-capacity monetization is a new revenue line for struggling European OEM plants and a fast, low-capex entry route for Chinese brands — watch for more such deals.
insights.locator: In addition to frontloading investments

insights.claim: Geely is already using part of Ford's plant near Valencia to produce vehicles for the European market, allowing it to avoid the high tariffs on shipments from China.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Live proof that contract manufacturing neutralizes EV tariffs without triggering investment screening — the loophole regulators have not yet closed.
insights.locator: Geely is already using part of Ford's plant near Valencia

insights.claim: It remains unresolved how Canada would treat contract manufacturing, which adopts a different cooperative structure than the majority-Canadian joint venture Ottawa says it wants — a regulatory gap in the middle of Canada's stated strategy.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The structure most likely to actually get built in Canada is the one least covered by policy — a source of approval risk for any announced deal.
insights.locator: It also remains to be seen how contract manufacturing

insights.claim: A new Chinese regulatory framework for overseas investments effective July 1, 2026 explicitly prohibits unauthorized cross-border transfers of personnel, expertise and technical know-how, with broad discretion over which sectors fall in scope.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Kills the premise of host-country technology-transfer conditions: Beijing has legally prohibited what the EU's IAA demands, so both cannot be satisfied.
insights.locator: A new regulatory framework for overseas investments

insights.claim: Two Chinese State Council supply-chain security decrees issued in April 2026 expanded authority to counter foreign sanctions and safeguard critical supply chains, and empower authorities to impose exit restrictions on employees of foreign companies who facilitate foreign sanctions targeting China.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Personal exit-ban exposure for compliance staff at multinationals operating in China is a concrete, underpriced operational risk.
insights.locator: These provisions come on the heels of two supply chain security decrees

insights.claim: Beijing's assertiveness may dampen prospects for Chinese EV firms to transfer technology to Western partners and limit which technologies Chinese firms can deploy in foreign markets, and despite widespread Western interest, substantive evidence of technology transfer remains limited in practice with no substantive tech-transfer deal yet realized.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Discount any host-government promise of Chinese technology transfer; the observed base rate is zero, which undercuts the industrial-policy case for these deals.
insights.locator: In particular, Beijing's more assertive behavior

insights.claim: Chinese authorities are unlikely to support major investments in jurisdictions perceived as hostile to Chinese commercial interests, so host governments seeking Chinese capital may need to offer stronger assurances of fair and consistent treatment — elevating political signalling over legal conditionality.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Implies Canada's welcoming-signal model may ultimately outperform the EU's rules model on deal volume, even if it captures less value per deal.
insights.locator: This dynamic may elevate the significance of political signaling

insights.claim: China may increasingly insist on market access as the price for investment, meaning countries that seek Chinese manufacturing while limiting Chinese imports will find the two objectives difficult to separate.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Predicts the shape of future deals: expect import-quota concessions to be bundled with any Chinese plant announcement in the EU as they already were in Canada.
insights.locator: Third, China may increasingly insist on market access

themes.theme: USMCA uncertainty is blocking Canadian deals

insights.claim: The US decision at the July 1, 2026 joint review not to extend USMCA in its current form leaves the agreement in effect but moving into annual reviews until the parties agree to extend it or it expires in 2036, adding recurring uncertainty over auto rules of origin.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Annual-review purgatory means North American auto investment decisions now carry a permanent one-year political horizon — a structural discount on Canadian and Mexican plant economics.
insights.locator: The U.S. decision at the July 1 joint review

insights.claim: US trade chief Jamieson Greer has advocated higher thresholds for US-made parts and tightened rules on Chinese content in USMCA autos, so even Canadian-built vehicles could lose US market access if they contain Chinese content.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: This is the core reason Chinese EV investment in Canada is stalled — the export option that justifies a Canadian plant may be legislated away.
insights.locator: This will add uncertainty on hot-button issues

insights.claim: On July 20, 2026 the White House announced new 50% tariffs on more than 500 categories of Canadian goods under Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, effective in 30 days, and asserts they apply regardless of whether goods are covered by USMCA.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: USMCA compliance no longer guarantees tariff exemption — this removes the central assumption underpinning integrated North American auto supply chains.
insights.locator: For instance, on July 20, the White House announced

insights.claim: Without greater predictability, firms may be increasingly reluctant to invest in Canada and instead prioritize jurisdictions where the regulatory and trade environments are more certain.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Expect continued Canadian FDI underperformance versus the EU in EV manufacturing until USMCA and US tariff policy stabilize.
insights.locator: More broadly, ongoing uncertainty over U.S. tariffs

insights.claim: Regional trade uncertainty is already redirecting capital: BYD cancelled a planned Mexican EV factory last year over geopolitical tensions and shifting trade policy, GAC will assemble in Mexico from the second half of this year but only for the Mexican market, and Toyota is spending US$3.6 billion to move production from Mexico to Texas.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Three concrete data points showing tariff risk is pulling auto capacity inside US borders — a reshoring signal with measurable dollar amounts.
insights.locator: To illustrate the complexity of the environment

insights.claim: Some in Ottawa may view the prospect of Chinese investment as leverage in negotiations with Washington over the USMCA review and bilateral tariffs, although US officials have accused Canada of sending mixed messages by courting Chinese capital while pledging to support North American reindustrialization.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Canada's China opening is partly a bargaining chip against Washington, which means it could be traded away — do not treat the EV quota as permanent.
insights.locator: Some in Ottawa may also see the prospect of Chinese investment

themes.theme: Hormuz demand shock and the strategic lesson

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz energy crisis has caused fuel price volatility and supply insecurity that made consumer demand for EVs skyrocket, sharpening the dilemma for the EU and Canada because meeting that demand with imported Chinese vehicles could further decimate domestic industries.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: An oil-shock-driven EV demand surge collides with protectionism — the tension resolves either as faster Chinese import penetration or as consumer price inflation in the West.
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz energy crisis has reinforced the urgency

insights.claim: Chinese firms possess both capital and willingness to invest in overseas production capacity at a time when many reindustrializing governments face fiscal constraints and limited private-sector appetite for large manufacturing investments, so Chinese money can substitute for public subsidy.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The fiscal argument for accepting Chinese capex will strengthen as Western budgets tighten — a directional bet that conditionality gets diluted over time.
insights.locator: Many governments that are pursuing reindustrialization strategies

insights.claim: The EU built detailed conditions largely after Chinese firms had already established a local presence in EVs, while Canada still lacks flagship investments despite a case-by-case engagement approach — meaning neither sequencing has yet produced the intended outcome.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sequencing is the variable that decides who captures value: rules imposed after entry grandfather incumbents; rules absent before entry attract nothing.
insights.locator: First, the EU and Canada illustrate trade-offs

insights.claim: EU scrutiny has intensified over de-industrialization and the prospect of a 'China shock 2.0' — a surge of subsidized Chinese high-tech exports — raising pressure on policymakers to reconcile investment benefits with security concerns.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The 'China shock 2.0' framing is the political engine behind further EU trade defence measures; expect more antidumping cases and sectoral instruments.
insights.locator: In the EU, however, scrutiny has intensified

insights.claim: There is no single right approach to managing Chinese investment; what matters most is a framework that is consistent, transparent and predictable, because long-term capital commitments require policy stability and regulatory clarity.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Predictability, not restrictiveness, is the variable to score when comparing jurisdictions for EV supply-chain capex.
insights.locator: The experiences of both Canada and the EU suggest

insights.claim: EU-China relations were near boiling point in June 2026, with Chinese officials abruptly cancelling two high-level meetings amid a surging EU trade deficit and new antidumping investigations, before Commerce Minister Wang Wentao's late-June Brussels visit produced only a trade-flow monitoring mechanism and an October deadline for tangible results.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: October 2026 is a hard checkpoint for EU-China trade escalation — a dated catalyst for European exporters and Chinese EV tariff policy.
insights.locator: While Joly toured BYD's Changzhou production site
